q: How many lobes does the right lung of a human have?
o: Two
Three
Four
Five
x: The right lung has three lobes (upper, middle and lower). The left lung has only two lobes because part of the space on the left is taken up by the heart.

q: The left lung is slightly smaller than the right lung mainly because:
o: The liver pushes up beneath it
It receives no branch of the pulmonary artery
Its alveoli are smaller than those of the right lung
It has a hollow (cardiac notch) that makes room for the heart
x: The heart lies slightly to the left in the thorax, so the left lung has a cardiac notch and only two lobes. The liver lies under the right side, and both lungs receive a pulmonary artery.

q: The glottis is:
o: The leaf-shaped flap of cartilage above the larynx
The point where the trachea divides into two bronchi
The opening between the vocal cords in the larynx
The passage joining the nasal cavity to the pharynx
x: The glottis is the slit-like opening between the vocal cords through which air enters the trachea. The flap that covers it during swallowing is the epiglottis, a different structure.

q: At its lower end, the trachea divides into:
o: Many bronchioles that open straight into alveoli
Three bronchi, one for each lobe of the right lung
Two primary bronchi, one going to each lung
Two alveolar ducts, one for each lung
x: The trachea branches into a right and a left primary (main) bronchus, one for each lung. These then branch further inside the lungs into smaller bronchi and bronchioles.

q: Inside the right lung, the right primary bronchus divides into how many secondary (lobar) bronchi?
o: Three
Two
Four
Ten
x: Each secondary (lobar) bronchus supplies one lobe. The right lung has three lobes, so it has three lobar bronchi; the left lung, with two lobes, has two.

q: A boy with a blocked nose breathes only through his mouth for several days. Compared with nose breathing, the air reaching his trachea is:
o: Warmer, moister and cleaner
Richer in oxygen and lower in carbon dioxide
Cooler, drier and less well filtered
Exactly the same, because the pharynx does all the conditioning
x: The nasal cavity, with its hairs, mucus and rich blood supply, cleans, warms and moistens air. The mouth does this far less, so mouth-breathed air is cooler, drier and dirtier. Its oxygen content is unchanged.

q: Goblet cells in the lining of the respiratory tract secrete:
o: Mucus
Surfactant
Pleural fluid
Digestive enzymes
x: Goblet cells are single-celled glands in the ciliated lining of the airways; they secrete sticky mucus that traps dust and microbes. Surfactant is made by cells in the alveolar wall, not by goblet cells.

q: The airways can be divided into a conducting part and a respiratory (gas-exchange) part. Which structures belong to the respiratory part?
o: Respiratory bronchioles, alveolar ducts and alveoli
Trachea, bronchi and bronchioles
Larynx, trachea and primary bronchi
Nasal cavity, pharynx and larynx
x: Gas exchange takes place only where there are alveoli: the respiratory bronchioles, alveolar ducts and alveolar sacs. The nose, pharynx, larynx, trachea, bronchi and terminal bronchioles only conduct air.

q: Alveolar macrophages (dust cells) found in the alveoli function to:
o: Secrete mucus to keep the alveoli moist
Carry oxygen from the alveoli to the capillaries
Engulf dust particles and microbes that reach the alveoli
Contract to push air out of the alveoli
x: Macrophages wander over the alveolar surface and engulf particles and bacteria that escape the mucus and cilia higher up. Oxygen crosses by diffusion, and alveoli have no contractile cells.

q: The layer of the pleura that is attached directly to the surface of the lung is the:
o: Parietal pleura
Pericardium
Peritoneum
Visceral pleura
x: The visceral pleura covers the lung itself, while the parietal pleura lines the inside of the thoracic wall and diaphragm. The pericardium surrounds the heart and the peritoneum lines the abdomen.

q: A stab wound lets outside air enter the pleural cavity on one side of the chest. The lung on that side collapses because:
o: The pressure around it is no longer lower than the pressure inside it, so its elastic tissue recoils
Its alveoli fill with blood and can no longer hold air
The diaphragm on that side stops receiving nerve impulses
The trachea is pushed shut by the air in the wound
x: Normally the pleural pressure is below the pressure in the lungs, which keeps the elastic lungs stretched against the chest wall. When air enters the pleural cavity this pressure difference is lost and the lung recoils and collapses.

q: At the very end of a quiet inspiration, just before expiration begins, the air pressure inside the alveoli is:
o: Much higher than atmospheric pressure
Equal to atmospheric pressure
Lowest of the whole breathing cycle
Zero
x: Air flows in only while alveolar pressure is below atmospheric pressure. At the end of inspiration air flow stops, which means the two pressures have become equal. The lowest pressure occurs during inspiration, not at its end.

q: During normal expiration, the diaphragm:
o: Contracts and moves downwards
Relaxes and returns to its upward dome shape
Contracts and becomes dome-shaped
Stays flat and does not move
x: In expiration the diaphragm muscle relaxes and is pushed back up into its dome shape by the abdominal organs, reducing the volume of the thorax. It is during inspiration that it contracts and flattens.

q: Impulses from the respiratory centre reach the diaphragm through the:
o: Vagus nerves
Optic nerves
Spinal accessory nerves
Phrenic nerves
x: The phrenic nerves carry motor impulses to the diaphragm, making it contract during inspiration. The vagus nerves mainly carry sensory information from the lungs back to the brain.

q: Which change in the blood is detected by the carotid and aortic bodies but NOT by the central chemoreceptors of the medulla?
o: A large fall in the oxygen level
A rise in the carbon dioxide level
A rise in the hydrogen ion concentration
A fall in the pH of cerebrospinal fluid
x: The central chemoreceptors respond to carbon dioxide through the H⁺ it forms; they are not sensitive to oxygen. A marked fall in blood oxygen is sensed by the peripheral chemoreceptors in the carotid and aortic bodies.

q: After deliberately breathing very fast and deep for a minute, a person may stop breathing for a short time without discomfort. This is because:
o: The blood has become saturated with carbon dioxide
The carbon dioxide level of the blood has fallen, so the respiratory centre is less stimulated
The diaphragm muscle is fatigued and cannot contract
The oxygen level of the blood has fallen sharply
x: Over-breathing washes carbon dioxide out of the blood. As CO₂ is the main stimulus for breathing, the drive to breathe falls until CO₂ builds up again. Blood oxygen actually rises slightly, not falls.

q: When the lungs are well inflated, stretch receptors in the walls of the bronchioles send impulses to the brain that:
o: Start a cough to clear the airways
Increase the rate and depth of inspiration
Stop inspiration so that the lungs are not over-inflated
Close the epiglottis over the glottis
x: Stretch receptors send impulses along the vagus nerve to the respiratory centre, which switches off inspiration and lets expiration begin (the Hering–Breuer reflex). This protects the lungs from over-stretching.

q: A person can hold a breath or speak a long sentence, overriding the normal breathing rhythm for a short time. This voluntary control comes from the:
o: Medulla oblongata alone
Cerebrum (cerebral cortex)
Cerebellum
Spinal cord alone
x: The automatic rhythm is set by the medulla, but the cerebral cortex can send voluntary impulses to the breathing muscles for a while. The cerebellum coordinates posture and movement, not voluntary breathing.

q: Sneezing clears irritants from the nasal cavity, whereas coughing clears them mainly from the:
o: Alveoli and alveolar ducts
Larynx, trachea and bronchi
Oesophagus and stomach
Pleural cavity
x: Coughing is a reflex set off by irritation of the larynx, trachea and bronchi; a forceful blast of air drives the irritant out through the mouth. Particles in the alveoli are removed by macrophages instead.

q: The scroll-like bony projections (conchae) on the side walls of the nasal cavity help the nose to condition air by:
o: Increasing the area of moist, blood-rich lining over which the air passes
Producing sound when air passes over them
Closing the nasal cavity during swallowing
Absorbing oxygen directly into the blood
x: The conchae make the air swirl over a large surface of moist mucous membrane with many blood vessels, so the air is warmed, moistened and filtered. No gas exchange happens in the nose.

q: Which is the correct sequence of events in normal quiet expiration?
o: Muscles contract → volume of thorax increases → pressure in lungs falls → air flows out
Muscles relax → volume of thorax increases → pressure in lungs rises → air flows out
Muscles relax → volume of thorax decreases → pressure in lungs rises above atmospheric → air flows out
Muscles contract → volume of thorax decreases → pressure in lungs falls below atmospheric → air flows out
x: In quiet expiration the diaphragm and external intercostals relax, the thoracic volume falls, the lungs recoil and the pressure inside them rises above atmospheric, so air moves out. Air always flows from higher to lower pressure.

q: If a person's diaphragm were paralysed but the external intercostal muscles still worked normally, the person would:
o: Be completely unable to breathe in
Breathe in more deeply than normal
Be able to breathe in only by contracting the internal intercostals
Still be able to breathe in, but less deeply than normal
x: Inspiration is produced by both the diaphragm and the external intercostals. With the diaphragm out of action, raising the ribs alone can still enlarge the thorax, but by less, so breaths are shallower. Internal intercostals help forced expiration, not inspiration.

q: In the neck, the larynx (voice box) lies between the:
o: Trachea and the bronchi
Pharynx and the trachea
Nasal cavity and the pharynx
Bronchi and the bronchioles
x: Air passes from the pharynx into the larynx and then down into the trachea. The larynx sits at the top of the trachea and contains the vocal cords.

q: Blood that has been oxygenated in the lungs returns to the heart through the:
o: Pulmonary veins, into the left atrium
Pulmonary arteries, into the right atrium
Venae cavae, into the right atrium
Aorta, into the left ventricle
x: The pulmonary veins are the only veins that carry oxygen-rich blood; they empty into the left atrium. The pulmonary arteries carry deoxygenated blood from the right ventricle to the lungs.

q: The rate at which oxygen diffuses across the alveolar wall into the blood would INCREASE if:
o: The alveolar wall became thicker
The total surface area of the alveoli became smaller
Blood flow through the pulmonary capillaries stopped
The difference in oxygen partial pressure across the wall became larger
x: Diffusion is faster with a larger concentration (partial pressure) gradient, a larger surface area and a thinner barrier. A thicker wall, a smaller area or stopped blood flow would all slow it.

q: Continuous flow of blood through the capillaries around the alveoli helps gas exchange because it:
o: Pushes oxygen actively into the red blood cells
Makes the alveolar walls thinner
Adds carbon dioxide to the alveolar air by active transport
Carries oxygenated blood away, keeping a steep oxygen gradient
x: As fresh deoxygenated blood keeps arriving and oxygenated blood keeps leaving, the oxygen level in the capillary stays lower than in the alveolus, so diffusion continues. No active transport is involved.

q: Breathing movements (ventilation) help gas exchange in the alveoli mainly by:
o: Pumping oxygen directly into the blood
Making the alveolar walls more permeable
Raising the temperature of alveolar air
Keeping the oxygen level high and the carbon dioxide level low in alveolar air
x: Ventilation constantly brings in fresh air and removes stale air, so oxygen in the alveoli stays higher and carbon dioxide lower than in the blood. This maintains the gradients for diffusion.

q: Lungs made of millions of tiny alveoli exchange gases far better than lungs made of a few large air sacs of the same total volume. The main reason is that tiny alveoli:
o: Hold a much larger volume of air
Have thicker, stronger walls
Need no blood supply
Provide a much larger total surface area
x: Dividing the same volume into many small sacs greatly increases the surface area available for diffusion. Alveoli have extremely thin walls and a dense network of capillaries.

q: Deoxygenated blood returning from the body tissues and arriving at the lungs normally has an oxygen partial pressure of about:
o: 100 mm Hg
160 mm Hg
0 mm Hg
40 mm Hg
x: Blood arriving in the pulmonary capillaries has a pO₂ of about 40 mm Hg, while alveolar air is about 100 mm Hg; this gradient drives oxygen into the blood. 160 mm Hg is the pO₂ of atmospheric air.

q: In a healthy person at rest, the haemoglobin in arterial blood leaving the lungs is about:
o: 50% saturated with oxygen
25% saturated with oxygen
97% saturated with oxygen
10% saturated with oxygen
x: At the alveolar pO₂ of about 100 mm Hg, haemoglobin becomes almost fully (about 97%) saturated. Mixed venous blood at rest is still about 75% saturated.

q: At rest, blood returning from the tissues to the lungs is still about 75% saturated with oxygen. This shows that:
o: The tissues cannot use oxygen from haemoglobin
Only about a quarter of the oxygen carried is given up at rest, leaving a reserve for activity
Most oxygen reaches the tissues dissolved in plasma
The lungs fail to load haemoglobin fully
x: Blood arrives at the tissues about 97% saturated and leaves about 75% saturated, so only roughly a quarter of its oxygen is unloaded at rest. During exercise the low pO₂ in muscles releases much more of this reserve.

q: 100 mL of fully oxygenated arterial blood carries a total of about:
o: 20 mL of oxygen
2 mL of oxygen
0.3 mL of oxygen
50 mL of oxygen
x: Because of haemoglobin, 100 mL of arterial blood carries about 20 mL of oxygen. Only about 0.3 mL of this is dissolved in the plasma; the rest is bound as oxyhaemoglobin.

q: Only a very small part of the oxygen in blood is carried dissolved in the plasma because:
o: Plasma proteins destroy dissolved oxygen
Oxygen is poorly soluble in water
Dissolved oxygen is immediately exhaled
Plasma is too acidic to hold oxygen
x: Oxygen dissolves only slightly in water, so plasma alone could carry far too little. Haemoglobin in red cells raises the oxygen-carrying capacity of blood many times over.

q: The oxygen–haemoglobin dissociation curve is S-shaped (sigmoid) because:
o: Binding of one oxygen molecule makes it easier for the next ones to bind
Haemoglobin can carry only one oxygen molecule
Oxygen binds to the globin chains rather than the haem groups
Carbon dioxide is always bound to haemoglobin at the same sites
x: After the first oxygen binds, the shape of haemoglobin changes so the remaining haem groups take up oxygen more easily (cooperative binding). This gives the curve its steep middle section and S shape.

q: On the steep middle part of the oxygen–haemoglobin dissociation curve, a small fall in oxygen partial pressure causes:
o: Almost no change in haemoglobin saturation
A large release of oxygen from haemoglobin
Haemoglobin to take up more oxygen
Haemoglobin to bind carbon monoxide instead
x: The steep part of the curve covers the pO₂ found in respiring tissues, so a small drop in pO₂ there makes haemoglobin give up a lot of oxygen. On the flat upper part, small changes have little effect.

q: The fact that haemoglobin releases more oxygen when the carbon dioxide concentration of the blood rises is called the:
o: Chloride shift
Haldane effect
Bohr effect
Oxygen debt
x: The Bohr effect is the lowering of haemoglobin's oxygen affinity by CO₂ (and H⁺), which helps unload oxygen in active tissues. The chloride shift is the exchange of HCO₃⁻ and Cl⁻ across the red-cell membrane.

q: About what proportion of the carbon dioxide in blood is carried simply dissolved in the plasma?
o: About 20–25%
About 5–10%
About 60–70%
About 90%
x: Only a small share (about 7%) of CO₂ travels dissolved. Roughly a quarter is carried as carbaminohaemoglobin and the large majority as hydrogencarbonate (bicarbonate) ions.

q: In the pulmonary capillaries, hydrogencarbonate ions move back from the plasma into the red blood cells. At the same time, chloride ions:
o: Move into the red blood cells with the hydrogencarbonate
Combine with haemoglobin to release oxygen
Are exhaled into the alveolar air
Move out of the red blood cells into the plasma
x: In the lungs the chloride shift reverses: HCO₃⁻ enters the red cells to be turned back into CO₂, and Cl⁻ leaves to keep the charge balanced. In the tissues the movements are the other way round.

q: In active body tissues, carbon dioxide moves from the cells into the capillary blood because:
o: Red blood cells pump it in by active transport
Its partial pressure in the blood is higher than in the cells
Its partial pressure in the cells is higher than in the blood
Haemoglobin attracts it more strongly than oxygen
x: Respiring cells produce CO₂, so their pCO₂ (about 46 mm Hg or more) is higher than that of arriving arterial blood (about 40 mm Hg). CO₂ therefore diffuses into the blood.

q: Compared with inhaled air, exhaled air contains roughly:
o: 21% oxygen and 0.04% carbon dioxide
16% oxygen and 4% carbon dioxide
16% oxygen and 0.04% carbon dioxide
4% oxygen and 16% carbon dioxide
x: Inhaled air has about 21% oxygen and 0.04% carbon dioxide. Exhaled air has about 16% oxygen and 4% carbon dioxide, and is also warmer and saturated with water vapour.

q: Exhaled air contains more oxygen than the air in the alveoli. The reason is that exhaled air:
o: Is mixed with air from the airways (dead space) that took no part in gas exchange
Picks up oxygen released by the trachea
Contains oxygen made by red blood cells
Has passed through the nose, which adds oxygen
x: The last part of each inspiration stays in the trachea and bronchi, where no exchange occurs. On expiration this fresher air mixes with alveolar air, so exhaled air has a higher oxygen level than alveolar air.

q: Of a normal 500 mL breath, about 150 mL only fills the nose, trachea, bronchi and bronchioles, where no gas exchange takes place. This volume is called the:
o: Residual volume
Tidal volume
Inspiratory reserve volume
Anatomical dead space
x: The conducting airways hold about 150 mL of air that never reaches the alveoli; this is the anatomical dead space. Residual volume is the air left in the lungs after a maximal expiration.

q: A person breathes 12 times a minute with a tidal volume of 500 mL. If the dead space is 150 mL, how much fresh air reaches the alveoli each minute?
x: Only 500 − 150 = 350 mL of each breath reaches the alveoli. 350 mL × 12 = 4200 mL per minute. 6000 mL is the total air breathed, and 1800 mL is the volume that only fills the dead space.

q: The inspiratory reserve volume is the:
o: Air left in the lungs after a forceful expiration
Extra air that can be breathed in by force after a normal inspiration
Air breathed in during one quiet breath
Extra air that can be forced out after a normal expiration
x: Inspiratory reserve volume is the additional air taken in by a deepest possible breath beyond a normal inspiration (about 3000 mL). The extra air forced out after a normal expiration is the expiratory reserve volume.

q: The instrument used to measure lung volumes such as tidal volume and vital capacity is the:
o: Sphygmomanometer
Stethoscope
Spirometer
Haemocytometer
x: A spirometer records the volume of air breathed in and out. A sphygmomanometer measures blood pressure and a haemocytometer is used to count blood cells.

q: Which person is most likely to have a larger vital capacity than an average adult of the same height?
o: A person with emphysema
A person with a collapsed lung
A person whose diaphragm is weakened
A trained swimmer
x: Regular endurance training strengthens the breathing muscles and increases vital capacity. Emphysema, a collapsed lung and a weak diaphragm all reduce the volume that can be breathed out after a deepest breath.

q: A heavy smoker becomes breathless very quickly when climbing stairs. Which two effects of smoking together best explain this?
o: Carbon monoxide lowers the oxygen carried by blood, and damaged alveoli reduce the surface for gas exchange
Nicotine slows the heart, and tar widens the bronchi
Tar increases the number of alveoli, and carbon monoxide raises haemoglobin's oxygen release
Nicotine lowers blood pressure, and cilia beat faster
x: Carboxyhaemoglobin cannot carry oxygen, and breakdown of alveolar walls reduces the area for diffusion; both cut oxygen supply to the muscles. Nicotine actually speeds the heart, and tar does not widen airways.

q: Which change happens within about a day of a smoker stopping smoking?
o: Destroyed alveolar walls are fully rebuilt
Any existing lung cancer disappears
The carbon monoxide level in the blood falls towards normal
Vital capacity doubles
x: Carbon monoxide is gradually breathed out once no more is inhaled, so the carboxyhaemoglobin level drops to near normal within about a day. Alveolar damage from emphysema is permanent, and cancer does not simply go away.

q: Children who grow up in homes where adults smoke indoors are more likely than other children to suffer from:
o: Asthma attacks and chest infections
Better lung growth
Fewer colds and coughs
A larger vital capacity
x: Breathing in other people's smoke irritates children's airways and weakens their defences, so they have more asthma attacks, bronchitis and other chest infections. It does not improve lung growth or capacity.

q: Smoke rising from the burning tip of a cigarette (sidestream smoke) is harmful to people nearby because:
o: It contains no carbon monoxide but much more oxygen
It is breathed only by the smoker
Its particles are too large to enter the lungs
It is not filtered and contains high levels of harmful substances
x: Sidestream smoke goes directly into the air without passing through the cigarette or the smoker's lungs, so it carries high concentrations of tar, carbon monoxide and other toxins that bystanders inhale.

q: Nicotine raises the heart rate partly by stimulating the release of:
o: Insulin
Adrenaline
Thyroxine
Antidiuretic hormone
x: Nicotine stimulates the adrenal glands to release adrenaline, which speeds the heart and narrows blood vessels. Insulin, thyroxine and ADH are not the hormones responsible for this quick effect.

q: Nicotine acts on the nervous system by:
o: Blocking the release of all neurotransmitters
Destroying the myelin sheath of neurons
Binding to acetylcholine receptors at synapses
Replacing sodium ions in the axon membrane
x: Nicotine has a shape similar to acetylcholine and binds to its receptors on postsynaptic membranes, stimulating them. This action in the brain's reward pathways is linked to its addictive effect.

q: Smoking increases the risk of coronary heart disease mainly because substances in smoke:
o: Damage the lining of arteries, encouraging fatty deposits (atheroma) to build up
Make the heart muscle grow stronger
Dissolve existing blood clots
Lower the blood pressure
x: Nicotine and carbon monoxide damage the inner lining of arteries, making fatty plaques more likely to form and narrow the coronary arteries. Nicotine also raises blood pressure and makes clotting more likely, not less.

q: In a heavy smoker, 10% of the haemoglobin is present as carboxyhaemoglobin. By about how much is the maximum oxygen-carrying capacity of the blood reduced?
x: Haemoglobin bound to carbon monoxide cannot carry oxygen, so if 10% is carboxyhaemoglobin, about 10% of the oxygen-carrying capacity is lost.

q: Benzopyrene, a compound in the tar of tobacco smoke, is an example of a:
o: Vitamin
Carcinogen
Neurotransmitter
Respiratory enzyme
x: Benzopyrene is one of the best-known cancer-causing chemicals (carcinogens) in tar. It damages DNA in the cells lining the airways.

q: Besides the lungs, smoking also increases the risk of cancer of the:
o: Bones of the legs only
Mouth, larynx and oesophagus
Skin of the hands only
Retina of the eye only
x: Smoke and tar pass over the lining of the mouth, throat and larynx, and are swallowed into the oesophagus, so cancers of these parts are much more common in smokers.

q: A long-term smoker begins to cough up blood-streaked mucus and is losing weight. Doctors are most concerned that he may have:
o: A common cold
Lung cancer
Hay fever
Normal smoker's cough only
x: Coughing up blood with weight loss in a long-term smoker is a warning sign of lung cancer, which must be investigated. A cold or hay fever does not usually cause bloody sputum and weight loss.

q: A smoker with chronic obstructive lung disease blows as hard as possible into a peak-flow meter. Compared with a healthy person, the reading will be:
o: Lower, because the narrowed airways and weak recoil slow the outflow of air
Higher, because the lungs are larger
Higher, because extra mucus pushes the air out faster
The same, because peak flow does not depend on the airways
x: Peak flow measures how fast air can be blown out. Narrowed, mucus-filled bronchi and loss of elastic recoil in COPD slow expiration, so the peak-flow reading falls.

q: Which statement about smoking tobacco through a water pipe (shisha or hookah) is correct?
o: The water removes all harmful substances from the smoke
It contains no nicotine and is not addictive
It cannot cause any lung disease
The smoke still delivers nicotine, carbon monoxide and tar to the lungs
x: Passing the smoke through water cools it but does not remove nicotine, carbon monoxide or tar. A long shisha session can expose the user to large amounts of these substances.

q: Studies show that the lung cancer death rate of people who give up smoking falls steadily over the following years. This finding supports the idea that:
o: Lung cancer is mainly inherited
Lung cancer is caused by a virus spread between people
Continued smoking is a cause of lung cancer
Stopping smoking causes lung cancer
x: If removing the exposure lowers the risk, the exposure is likely to be a cause. This evidence, along with the dose-related rise in risk, links smoking causally to lung cancer.

q: A smoker who stops suddenly feels irritable, restless and craves a cigarette for some days. This is because:
o: Carbon monoxide levels in the blood have risen
Tar is being released from the lungs into the brain
The lungs have stopped working
The body has become dependent on nicotine
x: Nicotine is addictive; when it is withdrawn the dependent smoker has withdrawal symptoms such as craving and irritability. Carbon monoxide levels actually fall after stopping.

q: Which pair correctly matches a component of tobacco smoke with its main harmful effect?
o: Carbon monoxide: reduces the oxygen carried by the blood
Tar: makes the heart beat faster
Nicotine: forms carboxyhaemoglobin
Carbon monoxide: causes addiction
x: Carbon monoxide binds haemoglobin and lowers oxygen transport. Nicotine is the addictive stimulant that speeds the heart, and tar carries most of the carcinogens.

q: Many long-term smokers make a whistling sound (wheeze) when breathing out. Wheezing is caused by:
o: Air leaking into the pleural cavity
Vibration of the vocal cords during expiration
Fluid filling the alveoli completely
Air flowing through narrowed bronchi and bronchioles
x: When inflammation, thick mucus and muscle spasm narrow the airways, air rushing through them makes a whistling wheeze, especially on breathing out. The vocal cords produce speech, not wheeze.

q: A heavy smoker's blood test shows raised carboxyhaemoglobin and a red blood cell count above normal. The raised red cell count is best explained as:
o: The body's response to reduced oxygen delivery to the tissues
A direct effect of tar on the bone marrow making it cancerous
Loss of plasma water through the lungs
Destruction of red cells by nicotine
x: Because carbon monoxide reduces oxygen carriage, the tissues receive less oxygen; the kidneys respond by releasing more erythropoietin, which increases red cell production. Destruction of red cells would lower the count.

q: A lung tumour grows into a bronchus and blocks it completely. The most direct result for the part of the lung supplied by that bronchus is that:
o: Air cannot reach its alveoli, so no gas exchange takes place there
Its alveoli receive extra oxygen
Its blood supply is cut off by the diaphragm
It produces more surfactant than normal
x: A blocked bronchus stops ventilation of the alveoli beyond it, so that region can no longer exchange gases; trapped mucus there also makes infection likely.

q: Filter-tipped cigarettes are still harmful mainly because the filter:
o: Adds extra nicotine to the smoke
Removes all oxygen from the smoke
Removes only part of the tar and does not remove carbon monoxide
Makes the smoke enter the blood without passing through the lungs
x: A filter traps some tar particles but lets through gases such as carbon monoxide and much of the tar and nicotine. Smokers of filtered cigarettes still have a high risk of lung disease.

q: The cells lining the bronchi that are damaged by tobacco smoke are mainly:
o: Skeletal muscle fibres
Cartilage cells
Ciliated columnar epithelial cells
Red blood cells
x: The bronchi are lined by ciliated columnar epithelium with goblet cells. Smoke paralyses and destroys the cilia and later these lining cells may become cancerous.

q: A patient with severe emphysema caused by smoking has a bluish colour of the lips and fingertips. This is because:
o: Tar has stained the skin blue
Too much oxygen is carried in the blood
The blood leaving the lungs is poorly oxygenated
Nicotine has widened the blood vessels of the skin
x: With fewer, damaged alveoli, much less oxygen enters the blood, so a large amount of haemoglobin stays deoxygenated, giving a bluish tinge (cyanosis). Tar does not stain the lips blue.
